title: Reproduce a post
text: Every post on this site is a Quarto document with R code that reads data, makes charts, and writes the text you see. You can run it yourself.

title: Reproduce a post
text:
1. Install the tools

R (version 4.5 or newer)
RStudio (optional but convenient)
Quarto (version 1.9 or newer)

title: Reproduce a post
text:
2. Get the code
Clone the repository, or download it as a zip from GitHub and unzip it.
git clone https://github.com/gpberber/chartingwaterlooregion.git
cd chartingwaterlooregion

title: Reproduce a post
text:
3. Install the R packages
Open R in the project folder and run:
source("R/packages.R")
install_missing()
This installs every package used on the site. The exact versions used to render each post are printed in the collapsed Reproducibility section at the bottom of that post.

title: Reproduce a post
section: 4. Get the data for a post
text:
4. Get the data for a post
Each post folder has a script that fetches its data. Small cleaned files are already in the repository. Larger files are attached to a GitHub Release and the script downloads them for you.
source("posts/<post-slug>/R/01_get_data.R")
Replace <post-slug> with the folder name shown in the URL of the post, for example kitchener-school-collisions. The README in each post folder lists the original sources and their licences.

title: Reproduce a post
text:
5. Render the post
From a terminal in the project folder:
quarto render posts/<post-slug>
The rendered page appears in _site/posts/<post-slug>/index.html. Open it in a browser.

title: Reproduce a post
text:
Notes

No keys required. All data sources are public. If a data-fetching script ever needs a key, its README says so and explains how to get one.
Cached results. The repository includes Quarto’s _freeze cache, so you can render the whole site without re-running any R code: quarto render at the project root.
House chart style. Colours and the ggplot2 theme live in R/theme_cwr.R. Source it in your own scripts to make charts that match.
Questions. Open an issue if something does not work.

title: About
text:
Charting Waterloo Region uses open data to answer plain questions about the place we live: how safe is it, how well do city services work, how is the region changing. Each post takes one question, finds the best available public data, and shows what the numbers say in a handful of carefully made charts.
Every chart is built in R and every post can be reproduced from the code and data in the GitHub repository. See Reproduce a post for the steps.

title: About
text:
Who writes it
Posts are written by Greg Berberich.

title: About
text:
How the posts are made

Sources are public. Statistics Canada tables, municipal open-data portals, published reports. Each post lists its sources, with links and licences, in a data section at the end.
Charts follow one style. Direct labels instead of legends, no chart junk, the same three colours throughout: blue for Waterloo Region, red for a comparison such as Canada, grey for context.
Nothing is hidden. The code, the cleaned data, and the rendered results all live in the repository. Large files are attached to GitHub Releases so anyone can download them.
Everything is reusable. Text and charts are published under CC BY 4.0: copy, share, or republish them, including in the news, with credit to Charting Waterloo Region. The code is MIT licensed. Data stays under the licence of whoever published it.

title: Charting Waterloo Region
text:
Collisions near Kitchener schools



Open Data

Road Safety

Kitchener



Pedestrian collisions in Kitchener fell steadily from 2015 to 2022, near schools and everywhere else, and about half happened where traffic controls were already in place.





Jan 30, 2025

15 min




No matching items

title: Collisions near Kitchener schools
text:
Are the streets around Kitchener’s schools more dangerous than the rest of the city? This post looks at every reported collision in Kitchener from January 2015 to June 2022 and asks how many involved pedestrians, how many happened within 250 m of a school, and what kind of traffic control was in place where they happened.
The short answer: pedestrian collisions have been falling across the whole city, the area around schools is no exception, and about half of all pedestrian collisions happened at locations that already had a stop sign, traffic light, or crossing guard.

title: Collisions near Kitchener schools
section: Pedestrian collisions fell by more than half
text:
Pedestrian collisions fell by more than half
There were 231 collisions involving a pedestrian in the study period. The number per year fell steadily, from 42 in 2015 to 18 in 2021 (Figure 1). The 2022 figure covers only the first six months.








Figure 1: Collisions involving a pedestrian in Kitchener, by year.

title: Collisions near Kitchener schools
section: About half happened where traffic controls were in place
text:
About half happened where traffic controls were in place
Just over half of all pedestrian collisions (129 of 231, or 56%) occurred at locations with some type of traffic control in place: traffic signals, stop signs, pedestrian crossovers, or crossing guards (Figure 2).








Figure 2: Pedestrian collisions by the type of traffic control at the location.

title: Collisions near Kitchener schools
section: Collisions near schools follow the same trend
text:
Collisions near schools follow the same trend
Of the 231 pedestrian collisions, 28 happened within 250 m of a school on a school day between 6 AM and 6 PM. (One of these was within 250 m of two schools, so the school-by-school counts in Table 1 add to 29.)

title: Collisions near Kitchener schools
text:
Map of collisions near schools
The map in Figure 5 shows the number and type of collisions within 250 m of each Kitchener school on regular school days between 6 AM and 6 PM. Hover over a circle for the school name and click it for the collision counts. A circle with a number groups several nearby schools; click it to zoom in.








Figure 5: Collisions within 250 m of a school on regular school days, 6 AM to 6 PM.

title: Collisions near Kitchener schools
text:
Data and methods

Collisions come from the City of Kitchener open data portal and cover January 2015 to June 2022. Each record has a location, date and hour, the type of traffic control at the location, and whether a pedestrian or cyclist was involved.
Schools are the public (Waterloo Region District School Board) and Catholic (Waterloo Catholic District School Board) schools in Kitchener, geocoded from their published addresses.
Near a school means within 250 m of a school’s geocoded address, measured as straight-line distance.
School day means a weekday outside July and August. Pandemic closure periods (March to June 2020, late December 2020 to early February 2021, mid-April to June 2021) are treated separately as lockdown school days.

The full source list, with links and licences, is in the post’s README.






NoteReproducibility





Code and data for this post: posts/kitchener-school-collisions/ on GitHub. See Reproduce a post for the steps.
